items.title: MPs moving to restrict gambling ads in Canada
items.author: Teever
items.content:
This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

For T.S., a 22-year-old Ontario man recovering from a gambling problem, widespread advertising for online casinos and betting during sports broadcasts is "frustrating."

"Imagine you're an alcoholic and there was a beer ad during every show you watched," he told CBC News. 

His gambling started three years ago as a fun Friday night activity with friends, but escalated. 

One night last year he found himself locked inside a bathroom, losing it all — having bet away $14,000.

T.S., who CBC has agreed not to name, says he quickly sought treatment and hasn't gambled since. But during his spree, all those ads fuelled him to gamble more.

"It certainly … would trigger me to go back and place another bet."

Politicians in Ottawa are moving to curb the widespread advertising currently seen across sports broadcasts, social media and online video games.

WATCH | Sports gambling ads are everywhere. There's a push to change that:

The federal standing committee on Canadian heritage meets next week to vote on , a law that proposes to rein in the ads across the country, amid new findings of increased addiction and gambling-related suicides in Ontario.

CBC partnered with the University of Bristol to assess the 2026 NHL playoffs to count the numbers of logos and gambling messages.

Across seven televised games featuring Canadian teams, viewers faced 3,000 gambling messages. Ninety-five per cent of those instances included no information about harm reduction or age restrictions.

Raffaello Rossi, the lead researcher and a senior lecturer in marketing at the University of Bristol, says by reviewing every second of the game, his team found ads or logos appearing two to three times every minute.

Ads appeared on stadium rinks, jerseys, helmets and during commercial breaks.

WATCH | Researcher Rafaello Rossi on his findings:

"Advertising via logos around the stadium, on the jerseys, on the helmets is much more efficient, because you've got a lot of knock-on effects," he said.

"For example, if a news broadcast shows the highlights of a match, you will see these logos all across the sporting event. If somebody shares something on their social media, you will see those logos."

He says viewers are additionally seeing the emergence of ads for prediction markets. 

The new analysis also confirms little has changed since with Rossi's team in 2024 revealed viewers were bombarded with thousands of ads and product placements in five NHL games (up to three per minute). 

Rossi says that's because Canada is behind other countries in passing legislation to curb gambling advertising.

"Multiple countries since then have introduced quite strict regulations and restrictions on gambling marketing in sports. So, for example, in Belgium and Italy and Spain, there's almost entire bans on sponsorship during sports."

Proposed Canadian ad standards

If Bill S-211 is approved at committee next week, the legislation — which has already passed the Senate — would be presented for a third and final reading in the House of Commons.

"It is a national framework around sports betting advertising," says the bill's sponsor, Bardish Chagger, the MP for Waterloo.

She says limits on advertising are a way to address emerging harms, including growing rates of gambling addiction and suicide deaths, like those witnessed in Ontario after the province allowed private online casinos and sports betting in 2022.

MP Bardish Chagger is sponsoring a bill launched by Sen. Marty Deacon to restrict gambling ads. The standing committee on Canadian heritage is set to vote on the bill in late October.(Dave Seglins/CBC)

"People are being impacted in a very harmful way. They are losing their livelihoods, they're losing their homes, they're losing their savings, they're losing their lives," Chagger told CBC News.

Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate and says it is time Canada tackles some of the negative public impacts of online gambling.

"These ads are ubiquitous across the country, especially in national broadcasts that are sponsored by betting companies, with logos plastered across broadcast desks, arenas and fields; this encourages Canadians in every province to gamble, even in those provinces who have held back," she wrote in an email to CBC News.

"We know where this is going, but we're allowing it to happen anyway."

Sen. Marty Deacon first spearheaded the bill in the Senate, where it has passed.(Twitter)

Current Canadian regulations are supposed to restrict gambling advertising targeting minors, at-risk people and gamblers who have asked to be excluded from the sites.

But the code doesn't go as far as some European countries, which have outright banned televised promotions on sportswear and during events.  

Belgium, the Netherlands, the U.K., France and Germany have imposed time-of-day bans on gambling advertisements, restricting them to after 9 p.m.

In France, companies have to get approval for their promotional strategies from the regulatory authority and submit an annual action plan to curb addiction. 

While Canada's Bill S-211 isn’t prescriptive, it asks the federal government to acknowledge the harms of online gambling and hold consultations to craft stricter regulations. 

Toronto Maple Leafs celebrate a goal flanked by advertising for Jackpot City online casino.(Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Chagger says she hopes her bill will eventually lead to a ban on gambling promotions on sportswear and during live sporting events, outlaw ads during certain hours and prohibit celebrities and athletes from collaborating with gambling companies.  

Ontario and Alberta oppose the federal bill.

In a letter to the federal government, Minister of Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction Dale Nally said the bill creates a two-tier regulatory system and threatens future provincial revenues.

Ontario's Attorney General Doug Downey wrote to the federal government earlier this year, saying that the province should be left to regulate ads.

"Ontario has already established comprehensive and modern regulatory framework for online gaming and sports betting, which came into force in 2022. Advertising standards and protections were a central component of this work," he wrote.

"The entire world is grappling with this in some way," said Matthew Young, a leading gambling researcher at Greo Evidence Insights.

"The real challenge right now is that we have a regulatory regime that is built upon physical borders, but a product that doesn't respect physical borders."

Addictions researcher Matthew Young is calling for limits on gambling ads and better monitoring of harms.(Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)

"The argument that it's provincial and territorial jurisdiction was all fine and well until ads from Ontario blanketed the nation and then suddenly New Brunswick had to deal with ads from Ontario."

The Canadian Gaming Association (CGA), a national trade group representing 80 companies that run casinos and online sports betting, has opposing the plan to regulate gambling ads across the country.

Instead, the CGA wants the government to spend money on assessing the "underlying health challenges" of gambling addiction, and let provinces decide advertising standards for themselves."

"Unlike alcohol and cannabis, online gambling platforms, both regulated and unregulated, are readily accessible with just a few clicks. In this environment, advertising plays an important role in directing consumers toward regulated operators that are subject to stringent oversight, consumer protection requirements and responsible gambling standards," the CGA submission states.  

Recovering gambler T.S. says advertising for online casino games should be banned or require warnings, similar to rules for other addictive substances, like tobacco and alcohol.

"I think similar to cigarettes, you could put labelling on the apps themselves, as well as the ads: 'Here's what happened to Terry when he spent half his life savings on blackjack one night.'"

No CVEs yet and no fixed mainline or stable release; the skb_zerocopy fix is posted for review but not merged, KernelCare has a livepatch only for CloudLinux/AlmaLinux 10, the ksmbd race fix sits in the ksmbd maintainer tree, and an SMB Direct fix is in a branch aimed at Linux 7.5. items.title: Jailbreaking the Switch 2
items.author: ledoge
items.content:
You can get a copy of the exploit from the ns2jb repository.

ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.

To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in Dabney House who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.

The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:

Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.

The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.

That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.

WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.

Code execution through the browser

It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.

We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc. Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.

  • WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.
  • Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.
  • And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.

Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed, but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here.

While that runs, let’s explore other options.

Code execution through smilehax2

My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:

  • They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1 does not support PAC.
  • Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.

Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this Discord RCE. I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.

In particular, I’m interested in SmileBASIC. This is because it’s been pwned before, in smilehax, giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.

Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked position + count <= array.length, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:

Say we have a string array of length 4, and we run REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF. wraps to . As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than . The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32), pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.

This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the , operations on will treat the array backing as if it were a string.

Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of , the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of .

This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.

Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.

I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on audio and ldn. I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the NV service, probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?

  • It’s probably similar to the module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.

The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from , we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them. Other sysmodules like and look enticing because they have permission to map executable memory, but they don’t have large attack surfaces, especially from SmileBASIC. We’ll come back to them later.

Buffer overflow with path normalization

Paths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like , call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lol

We’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data. We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write.

From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the saved PID to 1. Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.

Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is . All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The interface for the module seems pretty minimal too. It seemed more fruitful to pursue a logic bug than to look for memory corruption in directly.

Let’s revisit that first point about serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?

Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as Nintendo Content Archives, or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable, , and program metadata, .

To load a program, the built-in sysmodule asks to open ExeFS, and replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem. also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:

  • Is Nintendo’s signature of ’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid?
  • Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?

Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:

  • the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;
  • the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;
  • the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;
  • the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;
  • those hashes fix the executable content.

In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.

Arbitrary r/w to native code execution

Indeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer for the loader’s first check, but the executable itself can be arbitrary. The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem, has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.

There are two writes we perform:

  • The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original and our replacement .
  • The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent from crashing.

These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?

The process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message, processes it. Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when processes a loader message.

With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a for!

Getting built-in sysmodule native code execution

What s do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s connection to copy the NPDM of any ordinary sysmodule or game.

We’ll use this capability to launch our own code using ’s NPDM. As mentioned earlier, ’s NPDM gives it permission to invoke kernel SVCs like SetProcessMemoryPermission, , and . In this case, we’ll use to create a writeable view of ’s existing code. We can also dump ’s code by reading this view.

These calls, however, require a handle to the process. To get a handle to , we’ll use our ARW to overwrite ’s 4-byte handle with and then call from SmileBASIC. The kernel interprets this value to mean “the current process’s handle”, so SmileBASIC gets ’s handle.

We can then send this handle to our custom process, who patches ’s code.

Arbitrary code execution with any ordinary sysmodule’s permissions seems really powerful. We can investigate hardware without first exploiting each device’s driver. I’m hopeful this will help the homebrew community make progress toward CFW.

In the short term, there are a few next steps I think would be interesting:

  • Porting the sysmodule exploit to WebKit. Now that we know what bug we want to exploit, being able to perform arbitrary IPC calls is not as valuable. We might be able to trigger ARW in by changing the data used by WebKit’s existing filesystem code.
  • This jailbreak is tethered, and we don’t currently have a way to compromise built-in sysmodules other than . is a built-in sysmodule, so SM skips service ACL checks from , providing the same capabilities as smhax. I wonder if we can find bugs in other built-in modules?
  • With native code execution in , we can orchestrate its crypto hardware directly. For example, it’s used for NCA4 decryption.
  • The exploit has also been tested on the Switch 1, but I haven’t gotten around to packaging it yet. It wouldn’t provide the capabilities of a modchip, but it wouldn’t require any external hardware.

For now, I’m excited to see all the upcoming Switch 2 homebrew, emulation, and modding.

items.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.author: alphax314
items.content:
I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what or should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videos

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is , Escape is and ← is and so on.

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

So I added a operation instead:

ROW_0 COPY 1
ROW_1 COPY 2  
ROW_2 COPY 3
...

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

The same trick covers clearing the screen, inserting and deleting lines in vim, and navigating man pages. You can also copy a row and then overwrite part of it.

Altogether, the model uses a tiny vocabulary of 333 tokens: 256 byte tokens, 64 row tokens and a handful of special operations. Decoding is grammar-constrained, so every prediction is a valid screen update.

That tiny vocabulary comes back later, when I squeeze the model into a browser.

Generating the training data

I initially looked for existing datasets of terminal recordings, including asciinema, but couldn't find one with the precise keystroke-to-screen alignment I needed.

Luckily it wasn't too hard to create my own.

The basic idea was to generate believable terminal sessions by running real commands inside Docker containers, recording every keypress and the screen after each one.

The synthetic recipe was:

  1. Randomize usernames, hostnames, prompt styles, terminal sizes.
  2. Randomize directories and files based on a fictional persona (developer, sysadmin, etc.).
  3. Pick 6–24 weighted activities (modify files, vim, python, tmux, etc.).
  4. Track state, so sessions mostly open files that exist.
  5. Type like a person: one keypress at a time, with tab completion etc. I set the typo rate to 1.2%, which is generous to me.
  6. 35% of sessions start partway through, forcing the model to learn to work from any state.

The terminal size was mostly 32×96, with some 24×80 and 40×120, so the model doesn't overfit to one size.

I kept expanding the dataset as the model became more capable, and finally landed on 336k episodes, which corresponds to roughly 2B tokens. For comparison, the base model saw around 18T tokens during training.

I used Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B as the starting point. I needed a small model to get close to realtime performance. Being a coding model, it had also already seen plenty of CLI usage.

I started off by doing straightforward supervised fine-tuning: give a screen history and a keypress, predict the screen delta produced by the real terminal.

Ordinary typing was learned quickly: a letter appears, backspace removes it, the cursor moves.

In longer sessions, though, errors started to compound: a mistake in a filename propagated through the rest of the session.

Learning from its own mistakes

To address this I took a page from DAgger, where a model learns from the states it visits rather than just the ideal demonstrations.

For each training example:

  1. Pick a point in a recorded session, usually close to the command that produces the output.
  2. Let the model predict the next 1-4 events.
  3. Compare the resulting screen with the real recorded screen.
  4. If the difference is small enough, construct a correction that repairs the model's screen on the next keypress.
  5. Continue training on the corrected frame and a few subsequent real events.

The delta takes the model's incorrect screen to the correct next screen. In essence, it learns to "repair" its own mistakes.

There's one important restriction: the model must have enough information to infer the correction. Any words introduced by a correction must have appeared on an earlier real screen or in the user's typing, not just in the model's own predictions.

For example, if the model misspells a filename that appeared earlier, I can teach it to fix that. But if it lists a filename it has never seen, I can't expect it to get it right.

Training on those examples would actually reward hallucinations, which I really don't need more of.

About a third of the sampled sessions produced useful correction examples. I repeated this in three rounds, each time collecting mistakes from the latest model.

Self-correction was one of the more effective training changes. Along with some additional training data, it improved PresetBench (defined below) from 24/47 to 38/47 at int4.

In total, training the model and its later refinements took roughly 75 GPU-hours on an RTX 4090.

I use three tests. has 106 commands across 24 handwritten bash sessions, scored by exact output. has 47 scripted cases drawn from failures I hit in the demo. Neither test appears in the training data.

The has 32 worlds. Each writes two random values to two files, then reads them back in separate sessions. A world passes only if both readbacks are exact, giving 64 readbacks overall. The names and values never appear in training.

How much does fine-tuning help?

Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, prompted

The biggest difference was memory: WorldTUI got 9/13 readbacks right, compared with 2/13 and 3/13 for the prompted models.

It's still far from a reliable filesystem. It handles familiar commands fairly well, but combining them in new ways can quickly break things. For example, after , running often doesn't show the appended line.

For a while I stayed away from autoregressive models altogether. A full redraw is around 3,000 tokens, and generating those one at a time seemed hopeless for something that's supposed to feel like a terminal.

But they just performed so much better than the alternatives I tried, so I gave in. With one token at a time, typing felt fine at ~38 ms per key, but anything that redraws the whole screen (, , ) took up to 12 s on my RTX 4090, exactly as feared. Plenty of time to reconsider whether I needed the manual. And I wanted this to run on my Mac, in near real-time.

What I'd missed was that most rows in a frame don't depend on each other, so there's no reason to generate them one after another. I run one batch element per row. Each gets the same previous history (including KV cache) but generates only its own update.

That changes the decoding cost from the sum of all rows, up to 3,000 steps, to the length of the longest row, roughly 100 steps.

The cursor then becomes its own step at the end that can see the whole set of row updates.

This required a matching attention mask during training, but the speed improvement was worth it. Large-frame p95 latency dropped from 6.7 s to 0.87 s.

Rows that can't talk to each other

This might sound too good to be true, and it was. The issue is that since rows are independent, they can't coordinate, which led to opening on row 3 instead of row 0, or several rows adding food for snake at once.

The solution was speculative decoding.

Normally speculative decoding uses a small model to draft tokens and a larger model to verify them. Thanks to causal attention, several tokens can be verified in a single forward pass.

Here I use the same model for both: the parallel rows produce a draft, which the model then verifies sequentially.

The verifier keeps tokens up to the first disagreement. From there it generates its own correction and re-proposes the remaining draft.

In the browser on my M4 Mac, typing a single character takes about 60ms. A larger update like takes 2.5s sequentially, or 0.9s with parallel drafting and verification.

I started with Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, which has roughly 494M parameters. I really wanted a web demo, so I needed to shrink it. The embedding table for its 151,936-token vocabulary is 136M parameters. I only need my 333 tokens, so I can drop almost all of it, which takes the model from 494M to about 360M parameters (990MB → 716MB).

I then quantized it to int4, which brought it to 208 MB.

The browser demo uses a custom JavaScript implementation of the Qwen decoder, with compute shaders written in WGSL and run through WebGPU. The shaders unpack the 4-bit weights during inference. Activations and the attention cache use 32-bit floats. All inference runs locally in the tab.

Distilling it into fewer layers taught me something about which layers memory depends on. The teacher was an earlier checkpoint, which scored 78/106 on ShellBench. Removing just layer 7 without retraining barely changed next-token accuracy: 99.3% fell to 98.9%. But exact memory readbacks fell from 64/64 to 0/64. These tests fed in the true history, so the failure wasn't caused by errors compounding on the model's own output.

My first distilled student kept every even-numbered layer, but used the final layer, 23, instead of 22. It still wrote plausible terminal output, but returned the right value in only 31/64 memory readbacks. It always printed one of the two values it had written, but picked the wrong one about half the time. That's chance, and it hadn't recovered after 480M training tokens.

That student had dropped layers 1, 7, 15 and 22. A 16-layer student that kept those four passed all 32 memory test worlds, with 64/64 exact readbacks. It still passed all 32 worlds at 4-bit, at about 138MB. There was a cost elsewhere, though: it got 65 ShellBench commands right against the teacher's 78. So a student can look fine and have quietly lost its memory.

In the end I gave up on distilling it.

This was the part I was most interested in. Generating a convincing directory listing is easy. What I wanted was to create a file, edit it, wander off, and come back to find it unchanged.

The first time I started tmux, opened a file in vim, changed it, saved it and then in a different tmux window read the updated contents with , I felt like Dr. Frankenstein: it's alive!

It was very important to me that this should work beyond the bash prompt, so I trained on vim, python, man pages, snake and even tmux.

In vim, it handles the mode switch on and lets me save, quit or go back into insert mode.

What really blew my mind was tmux: I can create multiple panes, do various things in each and jump between them. It's not perfect, but it's a small model.

It even manages environment variables and variable expansion.

Since the base model is a coding model, I was curious how it would handle the Python REPL. It makes a decent attempt: small additions are usually right, and list comprehensions return a list, though often with the wrong contents. It's also slightly forgiving of typos: launches Python, but doesn't.

I didn't allow the Docker containers internet access, so tools like lynx are fairly boring. Python can handle very simple operations, but anything harder produces answers that remind me of GPT-3-era hallucinations.

Sometimes, when I create nested directories, it gets lost and all of a sudden I'm in a different path. There's clearly a lot of room to improve consistency.

In my testing, the demo ran about 20× slower in Firefox than in Chrome. It uses WebGPU in both. I haven't managed to establish the cause.

As always with projects like this, I tried to solve it myself first and only then looked at how others had approached it.

WorldTUI is closer to the original ChatGPT terminal trick, except that it's trained specifically on keypresses and screen updates, including full-screen applications like vim and tmux.

I had a blast building this. Is it useful? Not really. But for a 360M-parameter model running in a browser tab, it's far better than I expected.

What interests me most is that it manages to maintain a somewhat consistent world without implementing any of the rules underneath.

It's obviously a pretty weak world model, and I'd love to see how far this approach could go with better consistency and a different way of generating screen updates, perhaps using diffusion instead of autoregressive decoding.

One experiment I want to try next is training on thousands of randomly generated applications, each with its own controls and rules. The idea is to see whether the model can learn to predict the behaviour of an application it has never encountered before, given enough contextual clues.

Try it here. It's a 208 MB download, runs entirely locally, and works best in Chrome. Try to break it, and let me know what you find.

I'll post the weights soon and add the download link here.

items.title: There isn't an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability
items.author: zkldi
items.content:
I know, I know. It's all you're hearing about. That, and the number .

Don't get me wrong, there's clearly a bug here and it really does matter. But this is easy to exploit. It is certainly nowhere near as easy as Log4Shell/Heartbleed/RoRYaml etc.

Putting this up here so people read it. You should patch your servers anyway. There a real vulnerability here, but exploiting it is significantly harder than people are making it out to be - it is certainly not as easy as e.g. log4shell.

Justify yourself, you lunatic!

I don't think this PHP vulnerability is that exploitable. I think that 5 years ago people would've understood this, but now people are being deluded by their LLMs telling them they have an exploit when they don't.

If you take a look at github right now, there are thousands, literally thousands, of "PoC" exploits for this vulnerability. One thing you'll notice about all of them though, is that they against a vanilla PHP instance.

Go ahead, stand up a php server you think is vulnerable in Docker and then . Don't get your LLM to do it. No. Run the script, yourself. The exploits don't work.

Where's the exploit, Lebowski?

I think that a lot of people had assumed that LLMs will be able to build an exploit chain instantly from reading the diff, and that even if this was harder to exploit than other exploits, LLMs would've levelled the playing field. Well. There's no working exploit. Now what?

When I think about "we're very fucked" CVE10s on the Internet, I think of the following vulnerabilities:

  • RoR YAML decoding (send a post body with bad yaml in it)
  • Log4shell (set your user-agent to ${jdni:ldap:})
  • Shellshock (copy env x='() { :;}; echo vulnerable' and edit to taste)
  • Heartbleed (ask for Content-Length 10000000)

The second these vulnerabilities made the news, there were botnets doing the rounds causing damage. And this was before LLMs! People have to write the botnets. With their hands!

It's been 10 hours since this vulnerability has been posted, and half the software world is looking at it, and lord knows 100,000 people have got their "superintelligence" on the case. Nevertheless, there's no working exploit. The ones doing the rounds are fake, or only work in a lab, because...

Script kiddies (and script adults, who have also switched their brains off) now all think that, well, they don't understand UAF chaining, but this Claude guy knows everything and can totally make an exploit.

Hilariously, this results in the LLM giving their younger-brother an unplugged controller. It says exploit all across the screen... and has some smoking gun transcripts... but it's modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability. Cheating!!

I just plucked these three because they were the ones with the most stars, but it goes on for miles and miles.

One really amusing thing in common with most of these "PoC"s is that they lean on "LFI", or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability. In non-php terms, their exploit chain requires the server to already have a severe code-level vulnerability.

The strangest thing is that so many people have independently made this extraordinarily weird defect in judgement. That is because they haven't independently made this decision. Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them, hence the bizarre distribution in logical errors.

There's something important to be said here about how many people have Claude/GPT make design decisions for them, and how AI is the primary decision maker in the world right now. You've got this bizarre case of "Decision Schelling Points" where a method of solving a problem is extremely overrepresented, because it's what Claude does out of the box.

It's especially bizarre in this case, where AI is inserting a vulnerability on the server... to prove that the server is vulnerable to your "exploit any PHP instance" attack!

So why was everyone so scared?

  1. A PHP core team member said that this was cataclysmic ("exploits will start appearing 15 minutes after the patch drops")
  2. We all deep down know that PHP is insecure
  3. The exploit video had an anime girl in it
  4. We all know that LLMs are looming over the internet like a 100 ton chekov's anvil, and we know that code isn't secure

And we've had things like this before, but not in the LLM era yet. Luckily for us, this doesn't seem to be that day. This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment.

EDIT: I have added my contact details to this post and fixed a broken link. I added the disclaimer at the top that you should still patch.

Earlier this morning, Railway detected anomalous activity involving systems that store customer environment variables. After further investigation, our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.

We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers. We have notified these upstream providers to revoke all keys proactively, as we take these kinds of events extremely seriously.

While our initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, we are nevertheless recommending that all users take the actions described below as a precaution to protect your systems while we complete our review.

As such, we strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity.

All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume.

As we confirm which accounts were affected, we will contact those customers directly by email with additional details.

We will provide new updates on this announcement, and on status.railway.com as we narrow the scope of impact.

items.title: Mistral Large 4
items.author: funnym0nk3y
items.content:
Today, we’re launching a public preview of Mistral Large 4. Unofficially ML4, very officially: . ML4 pushes the frontier of open-weight performance. You can try the preview API today on Mistral Studio. Weights drop end of this month.

ML4 is a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal model with 52 billion active parameters. It is our largest and most capable model to date, and it continues to improve rapidly as we refine it.

The model demonstrates exceptional performance across coding, agentic workflows, and multimodal understanding. It already achieves performance competitive with the strongest open-source models globally, while significantly outperforming any open-weight model developed in the US or Europe. On critical enterprise workloads, including cybersecurity, finance and law, we find it to be state-of-the-art among open models. In some domains such as visual grounding, it goes further still, surpassing even frontier closed models.

We will release the weights by the end of the month. Until then, we are red-teaming the model in real-world settings with cybersecurity leaders, vetted partners, and state authorities, who will access the same model with reduced moderation and expanded cyber capabilities.

Forged in Europe. Built for AI sovereignty.

ML4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s own datacenters in Europe. The public preview is served on that same infrastructure. It is a significant milestone in our long-term investment across infrastructure, research, and product development: state-of-the-art performance in critical verticals, delivered through open weights, designed to give customers control over their AI.

This is particularly important in cybersecurity, where provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies.

The model will be available across multiple regions worldwide, including a European deployment that Mistral operates end-to-end, independently of other digital service providers and under European law. Fun fact: a significant share of ML4’s training data was multilingual, spanning more than 160 languages, including every official language of the European Union. 

We’ve been working closely with leading enterprises across the world in finance, engineering, manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceuticals, science, shipping, public sector, and other mission-critical industries to train ML4. In fact, the model uses the same training, customization, and RL environment we offer our customers through Mistral Forge.

There is still more to come. As we work toward releasing the weights, we will share further details on the model architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology.

This model will also serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. In the meantime, we invite you to try the preview API and share your feedback with us on social media.

ML4 is one of the world's strongest AI models for cybersecurity. On the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, an independent evaluation of how well AI models find and fix security flaws in real software, it ranks among the top five models globally and leads open-weight models developed outside China by a wide margin. On one of the index's tests, which asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch it, ML4 scores 82%, the highest of any model. It also solves 93% of the challenges in Cybench, a set of 40 exercises drawn from security competitions, one of the highest scores reported for an open-weight model.

That top score reflects a practical advantage. Several leading closed models, including Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, score near zero on the same test because they refuse to perform the task. Yet defending software often starts with proving that a flaw is real, exactly the kind of work safety filters in closed models can block. This matters even more as threat actors increasingly jailbreak those same models to support offensive cyber activity: defenders need systems that can match those capabilities without being constrained by the same refusals. ML4 can do that work, and its capabilities extend beyond what it was explicitly trained for: in internal testing, it proved useful for analysing malware, prioritising vulnerabilities, and writing detection rules. For organisations that need sovereign, auditable AI for security operations, it will be able to run on private cloud or on-premise.

ML4 against the field : efficiently reasoning over diverse complex challenges
Malware reverse-engineering: solving an out-of-distribution investigation task

ML4 excels across software engineering, repository understanding, and complex terminal workflows, scoring 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

We also ran a blind human evaluation with Surge AI on coding quality: professional annotators rated model outputs on a 1–5 scale, with model identities hidden. ML4 Preview ranked second of five models (3.74), ahead of Kimi K3 (3.59), GLM-5.3 (3.60) and GLM-5.2 (3.40), and behind only Claude Opus 5 (4.22).

ML4 runs general-purpose agents that gather information, use tools, and produce finished deliverables across complex workflows. On AutomationBench — 657 business workflows across apps like Gmail, Google Sheets, Slack, and Salesforce — it scores 59.9%, ahead of Kimi K3, MiMo-V2.6-Pro, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.

It's just as strong on the professional deliverables that knowledge work actually produces: spreadsheets, slides, and PDFs. On AA-Briefcase, which evaluates long-horizon knowledge work, it reaches 1,393 Elo, ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro.

ML4 is a step change in the ability of our models to understand images. It reasons powerfully across complex documents, charts, and natural images, and brings vision to the industries where perception is critical such as engineering, manufacturing, and earth observation.

The model can further combine visual grounding with agentic capabilities: from inspecting gigapixel satellite imagery — helping disaster-response teams act when time counts — to analyzing engineering-drawings — zooming in, inspecting, and verifying until the answer is exact. In our demos above, ML4 grounds dense natural scenes, verifies mechanical parts in technical drawings, retrieves evidence from PDFs, and scans massive geospatial images for the hardest-to-find objects.

On visual grounding particularly, we find ML4 to be one of the most capable models we tested, for instance surpassing GPT-6-Astra on Dense 200 (42% vs 41%).

ML4 brings strong scientific capabilities, built by combining AI-driven methods with our researchers' expertise in mathematics, physics, and chemistry.

It's highly proficient at agentic coding for scientific tasks such as data analysis, modeling, and simulating physical reality, which lets researchers focus on the questions rather than the plumbing. In benchmarks, ML4 is state of the art on SciCode-Verified among open-weight models. In practice, it can generate a full Hartree–Fock simulation in one shot — a complex, multi-step chemistry task built from a series of advanced routines.

ML4's math is stronger too, in both formal reasoning and applied mathematics. In our human evaluations it reasons more precisely and with more structure than GLM-5.3, and it can sustain long, domain-specific applied-mathematics tasks, including work relevant to frontier theoretical physics.

Together, these capabilities make ML4 a strong research assistant across the full technical workflow — from the first question to the final result.

SciCode-Verified tests the capabilities of models to implement complex scientific workflows in code for domains such as physics, mathematics, material science and biology. 

Internal eval on STEM tasks (math and physics) of ML4 against GLM5.3

ML4 is our most capable model for the real-world tasks which professionals handle every day. It can create, edit and fix complex spreadsheets and documents, showing exemplary performance on both legal and financial benchmarks.

Notably, we evaluated ML4 through third party evaluators () on representative tasks for both legal and financial tasks, finding the model exceeds GPT-6-Astra in both cases. On HarveyAI’s Legal Agent benchmark, ML4 outperforms all open-source models.

FinWorkBench tests model capabilities at creating/editing spreadsheets on real life Finance and Accounting use cases.

Financial analysis demands precision and the ability to synthesize information from multiple sources, a process that remains time-consuming at many financial institutions today. In this demo, ML4 compared to other top OSS models take on the same multistep corporate finance challenge, searching through public company filings and financial reports, such as those available via EDGAR and equivalent European databases. An animated semantic map traces each model's journey toward a solution, highlighting every document retrieved along the way. Each track's position reflects the evidence gathered, the results of calculations, and the questions that remain unresolved. Viewers can follow how the investigations unfold and compare the distinct paths each model takes before arriving at its final answer.

ML4 has saturated our benchmarks on robustness to indirect prompt injections, putting it at the frontier of OSS models (compared to GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K2.6, Kimi-K3, DS-V4-Pro-0813). On Lakera’s public , ML4 resists 93.3% of attacks – we see no higher scores among competitors.

ML4 also engages more responsibly with users than any of our previous models. We highlight our results on the , where ML4 again sits at our highest measured score among OSS models (1.691, with 2 being the maximum denoted as “”). 

Of particular relevance is the model’s propensity to refuse malicious requests regarding cybersecurity. Despite strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, the average refusal rate of the model on cyber prompts from , , and is higher than all OSS models.

We ran an internal evaluation in which expert annotators across coding, computer-aided design (CAD), finance, mathematics and physics compared Mistral Large 4 with GLM-5.3. ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.

Reinforcement learning at scale

Base models are improving fast, and our post-training has to keep pace. A recipe tuned for yesterday's model leaves capability on the table with today's frontier, because ground truth samples that once pushed a model to its limits won’t anymore. We use Reinforcement Learning (RL) because it adapts as the model does: we train on the outcomes of the model's own attempts, and we can raise the difficulty and the breadth of the tasks as it gets stronger.

Our RL library was designed to make new environments easy to add and train at scale. A shared, composable interface allows a single training run to combine tasks ranging from single-turn chat and complex scientific problem solving to safety alignment, factuality, and long-horizon tool use. These environments share scaffolds and resources such as code sandboxes, web search, and external APIs. The same composability extends to verification, with reward models, unit tests, LLM judges, and static checks combined as needed for each task.

At runtime, an autoscaling fleet of actors generates tens of thousands of rollouts in parallel while model training proceeds asynchronously. The generation and training pipeline is optimized for long trajectories, supporting rollout budgets of millions of tokens across multiple compactions while keeping staleness low. Novel methods and optimizations across both stages minimize off-policy drift and enable stable RL over long horizons.

At our current scale (3k GPUs), a single training run produces roughly 33 billion tokens per day, of which around 16 billion are trainable completion tokens after filtering and masking. We can see the run progress directly in the training rollouts: training rewards rise across several representative environments as the policy learns to solve increasingly complex tasks. Below are a few examples.

The improvements are not specific to the environments we train on; they transfer to downstream evals, and the final model owes them to both post-training stages (supervised fine-tuning and RL), as shown in the charts.

This is only the beginning. ML4 is the first milestone on the roadmap funded by our €3 billion Series D — the largest equity round ever raised by a European technology company. That capital is already being put to work: we are significantly scaling up our compute capacity in our own European datacenters, and much more is coming online in the months ahead.

More compute means more training. The reinforcement learning run behind this preview is still in flight, and the model is showing no signs of saturation — there is substantial headroom ahead. As we scale up training on our expanded infrastructure, we expect large and rapid improvements in the weeks and months to come.

We will release the weights by the end of the month, along with more details on the architecture, additional benchmarks, and our post-training methodology. And ML4 is only the foundation: it will serve as the base for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models, built for the industries and workloads our customers care about most.

The pace of progress from here will be fast. Stay tuned.

On October 21, 2026, we released versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE).

These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already include these fixes and do not need to take action.

GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases: scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays. For more information, please visit our releases handbook and security FAQ. You can see all of GitLab release blog posts here.

For security fixes, the issues detailing each vulnerability are made public on our issue tracker 90 days after the release in which they were patched.

We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more best practices in securing your GitLab instance in our blog post.

We that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible.

When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected.

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression.

In addition to our standard patch releases, we have backported this fix to GitLab CE/EE versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9.

GitLab CE/EE: all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1 10.0 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H)

Thanks joaxcar for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

GitLab security has released two threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances, listed below. GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched.

CVE-2026-15723 - Improper Authentication issue in OmniAuth-to-LDAP auto-linking email lookup impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking were both enabled, an authenticated user could have taken over an existing LDAP-backed account without any interaction from the targeted user, due to improper input sanitization in the LDAP email lookup path used during OmniAuth identity linking.

Thanks stealthy for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-112212 - Cache Poisoning issue in OAuth/OIDC discovery endpoints impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, an unauthenticated user could have poisoned a shared cache’s OAuth/OIDC discovery document to redirect certain flows to an externally controlled server, due to improper trust of user-supplied values when constructing endpoint URLs in cached discovery responses.

This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Peter Arts

CVE-2026-12664 - Improper Access Control issue in GraphQL work item email address field impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with a read_api-scoped token to retrieve a project’s incoming email address and create work items, bypassing the token’s restrictions, due to insufficient scope enforcement on a GraphQL field.

Thanks go7f0 for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when the instance-wide SAML or LDAP membership lock was enabled, an authenticated user could have granted or accepted project and group membership outside the identity provider’s control, due to incomplete enforcement of the membership lock on requests created before the lock was enabled.

Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, an unauthenticated user could have retrieved sensitive internal server credentials due to improper filtering of internal response headers.

Thanks altair00 for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-13319 - Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key issue in group milestones API impacts GitLab CE/EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that could have allowed an authenticated user to read milestone metadata, including titles, descriptions, and full project paths, from arbitrary private projects across the instance without any project membership, due to missing authorization checks on a user-supplied project filter parameter in the group milestones API.

Thanks a0xnirudh for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

GitLab has remediated an issue that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user to access paid AI features without a valid subscription due to insufficient server-side validation in billing eligibility checks.

This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Halil Coban

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when a merge request in a public project referenced a confidential issue from a private project, an authenticated user with no project membership could have read the confidential issue’s title, due to a viewer-independent fragment cache key that incorrectly shared per-user-redacted rendered content across all users.

Thanks 20kilograma for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-14288 - Improper Access Control issue in merge request approval policy enforcement impacts GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that under certain conditions could have allowed an authenticated user to bypass a required merge request approval policy on a protected branch due to improper access control during approval rule synchronization.

Thanks 3nvz for reporting this vulnerability through our HackerOne bug bounty program

CVE-2026-112326 - Improper Cleanup on Thrown Exception issue in security findings impacts GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an authenticated user with read-only permissions to permanently delete existing vulnerability records due to improper cleanup logic that failed to distinguish between pre-existing records from newly created ones during error handling.

This vulnerability has been discovered internally by GitLab team member Gregory Havenga

CVE-2026-103515 - Improper Access Control issue in group Duo admin-lock enforcement for Amazon Q settings impacts GitLab EE

GitLab has remediated an issue that, when an instance administrator locked a group’s Duo availability, an authenticated user with group Owner permissions could have re-enabled AI-backed data egress to a third-party service for that group and its descendant projects, due to insufficient granularity of the admin-lock enforcement controls.

items.title: Meta ordered to pay $25B penalty in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
items.author: cbg0
items.content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026.
Brendan McDermid | Reuters

was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.

The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.

Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.

"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.

The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.

"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.

He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."

Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."

"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."

Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.

In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg-led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users, raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.

Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.

"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.

Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.

Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

items.title: EA is shutting down BioWare

items.content:
Through every major moment we’ve faced as a company, your commitment to creating awesome games and experiences for our players continues to be impressive. Together, we’ve built epic worlds and global communities that are part of the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest.

Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success.

As we focus on these larger opportunities, we’ve had a small team at BioWare working on early-development for Mass Effect. We’re sure there will be questions about what these changes mean for individual teams and for EA more broadly. You can speak directly with your leaders to hear more on that, and we’ll make sure to spend time discussing our direction and the work ahead at our next Global Town Hall in November.
